questions: How can psychological evidence help designers build technologies and interfaces around human needs?
Why do people trust, adopt, resist or change their behaviour around digital and automated systems?

alternatives.label: Psychology, cognition & technological systems
alternatives.labelReason: The completed programme combines sustained psychology/cognition/research with technical methods, product development and physical foundations; it does not claim to reproduce a full human-technology-interaction or Living engineering curriculum.
alternatives.concept: A related programme joining psychological and cognitive mechanisms, behavioural research and evidence synthesis with programming, data, intelligent systems, consumer-needs design and introductory physical foundations. Actual psychological experiments, a product-development project and computational work support investigation of people and technology. It differs from TU/e’s dedicated human-factors, environmental-psychology, building-services and spatial-design formation in the Living specialization.
progression: Actual current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites pass; first-year PPD,24unique180EC,fourperterm,advancedminimum. Foundationalrhetoric/data/empiricalmethods preferredbeforeadvancedapplications; no inventedformalprerequisites. Social Psychology precedes Persuasive Communication. Intro Brain/Behaviour supplies the formal cognitive foundation; later comparative Neurobiology adds rhythms/regulation rather than an invented prerequisite.

alternatives.label: Behaviour, responsible technology & digital society
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum keeps psychological and empirical study while emphasizing customer needs, organizational adoption, digital strategy, communication and responsible technology; shared physical foundations support actual product investigation.
alternatives.concept: A related programme examining how people adopt, resist and are affected by technology through psychological and qualitative research, product and customer-needs investigation, communication, organizations, digital strategy and AI ethics. Technical data/programming methods support this inquiry. It differs from the dedicated spatial/building engineering and environmental-psychology formation of the comparator’s Living specialization. Introductory physical and material investigation supports the shared consumer-product design work.
progression: Actual current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites pass; first-year PPD,24unique180EC,fourperterm,advancedminimum. Foundationalrhetoric/data/empiricalmethods preferredbeforeadvancedapplications; no inventedformalprerequisites. Social Psychology follows in year1 before persuasion/organizational study; Data Science precedes Machine Learning. Product Design is a final-semester applied project alongside customer research after research foundations. No new formal prerequisite invented.
alternatives.distinctness: 8 courses (60 EC)different eachway. The first deepens neuroscience, quantitative models, image/learning/robotic systems and physical foundations; the second emphasizes qualitative inquiry, customer/organizational research, communication, sociology, digital strategy and societal AI. Sharedpsychology/design/empiricalmethods anchorboth,notmerelabeldifference.

blocks: Introduction to Brain & Behavior supplies broad psychological and neuroscientific foundations, but not the target course's dedicated technology framing.
Social Psychology directly addresses social influence and behaviour; TU/e also gives environmental psychology dedicated coverage.
Neurobiology provides a biological account of brain and behaviour.
Higher Order Functions studies attention, memory, executive functions and decision processes.
Perception & Action closely addresses perception, action and sensorimotor interaction.
Introduction to Programming provides the computational foundation used in behavioural technology work.
Introduction to Data Science develops applied data preparation and visualisation.
Research Methods & Statistics covers research design, experiments, surveys and inference.
Partial behavioural-method correspondence through experimental/nonexperimental designs, multivariable inference, diagnostics and R reporting. This is not the entire TU/e research sequence.
Mathematical Methods covers calculus and quantitative modelling.
Both teach qualitative inquiry with collection and analysis of social experience. UCR is general social research, rather than the complete technology-specific qualitative project.
AI Ethics directly addresses responsible design, fairness, privacy and accountability.

Partial design-project correspondence through customer interviews, needs/specifications, product concepts and prototypes where feasible. UCR does not reproduce TU/e’s multidisciplinary engineering challenge.
Introduction to Sociology addresses institutions and social relations; TU/e adds dedicated social-network analysis.
UCR distributes societal and ethical analysis across several courses; no single scheduled course reproduces this ITEC component.
Elective space, formation and final project
TU/e requires an ordinary 10 EC final project. UCR optional independent research carries 15 EC and remains outside the scheduled 180 EC.
Perception, cognitive experiments and user-needs product design provide related human-focused methods, but no single selected course establishes the full dedicated Human Factors component.
AI ethics, psychological evidence and algorithmic methods contribute across the programmes; rational-agent planning alone does not establish a full human-centred AI course.
UCR includes actual empirical and statistical projects, but no single selected course is the dedicated technology-related quantitative project. Mathematical sampling algorithms are not that project.
UCR meta-analysis, experimental methods and ethical work provide advanced research contributions, but no single selected course establishes the full advanced-methods and research-ethics unit.
UCR introductory mechanics and physical models support foundations; they do not establish the full physics-for-engineers component.
Consumer-product models and prototypes do not establish a 3D spatial-modeling studio.
Introductory material and environmental concepts do not establish building circularity and energy-performance engineering.
Social, health and sustainability perspectives relate to human needs, but no selected course establishes the dedicated healthy/sustainable living-environment component.
No included course establishes building-services engineering.
Neurobiology includes biological rhythms and sleep and is already shown once; the selected courses do not establish environmental-lighting measurement and design.
15 EC of genuine approved elective space in year 2 remains open.
30 EC of genuine approved elective space in year 3 remains open.

notes.text: TU/e combines psychology and behavioural research with a 30 EC technical specialization and a required final project. The displayed Living route includes physics, spatial modeling, building circularity and services, healthy environments and lighting. UCR offers related psychological, cognitive, empirical, design and technological methods, but does not reproduce that building-engineering and environmental-psychology sequence, the full human-factors curriculum or compulsory final project.

provides Python programming and computational problem-solving for interactive technologies
develops data cleaning, visualisation and analysis for behavioural and technology evidence
establishes psychological and neuroscientific foundations for explaining behaviour
provides calculus, equations and mathematical modelling for technology and intelligent systems

develops image processing and computer vision for intelligent and interactive systems
Description supports neural perception and goal-directed action through cognitive-neuroscience/neuropsychology methods; no unrecorded built-environment design or lighting experiment assumed.
Actual systematic review/meta-analysis, effect sizes, heterogeneity/moderators/bias and R synthesis project support evaluation of behavioural evidence; not an original experimental final project.
develops neural networks and deep learning for intelligent technology

Actual arm/gripper programming, kinematics, collision planning and manipulation give technical robotic-system knowledge, with shorter sensing/control and a chosen human-robot/legal/ethics issue. Not the comparator’s spatial/building engineering sequence or full human-robot experiment.
examines planning and decision-making by intelligent agents under uncertainty
provides probability, estimation and statistical inference
Actual biopsychosocial health, treatment decisions, clinical-health cases and interviewing support patient wellbeing and behavioural needs; not digital-tool evaluation itself.
examines framing, persuasion, nudging and the ethics of behavioural influence

Description supports neuroscience/psychology of language production and comprehension, semantics, bilingualism and hands-on language experiments; relevant human-language mechanisms, not an interface-design course.
examines fairness, privacy, accountability and responsible AI design
uses design thinking and user problem framing to develop products and services
provides concepts for analysing technology within institutions and social relations
examines responsible digital transformation and organisational technology adoption
uses customer-needs research, product design and prototyping for user-oriented solutions
examines organisational behaviour, culture, decision-making and technological change
examines the organisational, economic and societal implications of AI
Description fully supports planning/conducting customer-opinion research and reporting findings. No unspecified qualitative technique or usability-design test assumed.
examines trust, public spheres and institutions shaping responses to technology

Actual physical/chemical principles, dynamic models and biopolymer strength/elasticity experiments support introductory technological/material reasoning; not building physics, energy-performance engineering or environmental psychology.

Actual interviews, focus groups, ethnographic/visual approaches, coding and team data collection/analysis support empirical inquiry into social experience and user perspectives; not guaranteed usability testing.

audience.programmeDescription: TU/e Psychology & Technology studies how people think, behave and interact with technology, combining behavioural science and research with engineering. The displayed Living specialization applies this to healthy, sustainable environments and buildings.
audience.comparisonExplanation: TU/e combines psychology and behavioural research with a 30 EC technical specialization and a required final project. The displayed Living route includes physics, spatial modeling, building circularity and services, healthy environments and lighting. curriculum.routeLabel: Living specialization; ordinary 10 EC final project
curriculum.limitation: Current adopted regulations and 2026 cohort curriculum; future offerings may change.

componentNotes.pt-bfp: Ordinary 10 EC final project over the third and fourth quarters of year 3. Entry requires 120 EC, including all compulsory first-year courses, and a pass in either Behavioural Research Methods II or Advanced Research Methods and Research Ethics. The optional 15 EC Innovation Space format is not added to this pathway.
componentNotes.pt-y2-open: 15 EC of open study in year 2, followed by 30 EC in year 3. At least 30 EC of the combined 45 EC must be at intermediate or advanced level, including 15 EC at advanced level. Content must not overlap. Submit a complete study plan for approval after earning 45 EC.
componentNotes.pt-y3-open: 30 EC of open study. Changes to the approved study plan require approval.
componentNotes.pt-itec-ethics: Engineering Ethics and Engineering for Society each carry 5 EC. Five Studium Generale activities and MyFuture activities with a combined value of seven add no credits. Personal and professional development is embedded in the core courses.
componentNotes.pt-multi-cbl: Requires completion of previously offered courses embedding communication, cooperation, planning and organization skills.
